questions.question: A girl returns from Honduras where she spent much time outdoors and has a painless, minimally erythematous expanding lesion of one week's duration on the upper fold of the pinna near its junction with the temple. [image-based question: skin lesion with what appears to be a breathing hole]
questions.question_raw: Q7 (2008). Picture of a girl coming back from Honduras where she spent a lot of time outdoors and has had an expanding painless/minimally red lesion growing for the last week on the upper fold of her pinna, near the junction with her temple. [image-based question: skin lesion with what appears to be a breathing hole]
questions.model_answer:
a) Furuncular myiasis due to Dermatobia hominis (New World human botfly). The Latin American travel history, an exposed-site lesion (face/pinna), the boil-like furuncular swelling, and the central punctum/breathing hole through which the larva respires via its posterior spiracles are characteristic; D. hominis is the predominant cause of furuncular myiasis acquired in the Americas and typically involves exposed areas (scalp, face, extremities).
b) Coax the embedded larva out by smothering its respiratory spiracles with an occlusive coating (petrolatum/Vaseline, clear nail polish, tobacco tar, pork fat, raw beefsteak, or bacon); injection of lidocaine into the lesion is an alternative extraction technique. If occlusion fails, the larva may be asphyxiated and require surgical or vacuum extraction. Then cleanse and conservatively debride the wound, give tetanus prophylaxis, and treat any secondary bacterial infection with antibiotics.

cohort_answer.text: Myiasis - from Honduras likely larva of Dermatobia hominis; region exposed consistent (scalp, face, extremities). Tumbu fly (Cordylobia anthropophaga) myiasis in central/east Africa affects covered body regions (buttocks, trunk); New World (Dermatobia hominis) myiasis affects exposed areas (scalp, face, extremities). Treatment: Occlusion of breathing holes with vaseline, clear fingernail polish, tobacco tar, raw pork/beef, or injecting lidocaine; failed occlusive therapy may require vacuum or surgical extraction; tetanus prophylaxis; counsel to monitor for secondary bacterial infections.
